A1-A2.headline: Texas Cotton Farms Need Water

pages.text: Farmers in Texas grow a lot of cotton. The year 2026 is very dry. This is a big problem for the farms. Many plants are dead now.
pages.caption: A satellite image of the same Lubbock region on September 9, 2026, appears parched, with much less green vegetation and mostly dry lakes.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Drought Monitor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln

pages.text: One farmer said 90 percent of her cotton died. Space pictures show the land. The land was green in 2025. Now the land is brown.
pages.caption: A satellite image of farmland around Lubbock, Texas, on September 22, 2025, features a patchwork of green and brown agricultural fields and several playa lakes with varying amounts of water.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Drought Monitor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln

pages.text: There is not enough water for the crops. Farmers use water from under the ground. This water is going away. There are small lakes in the fields.
These lakes are called playa lakes. They help keep the ground water full. Many of these lakes are dry now. Farmers need water to grow food. They are worried about the future.

evidence: "This is the first year that we've had cotton completely die," said Lacy Cotter-Vardeman , a farmer based in Lubbock County whose family has worked the land there for several generations.
"I was just talking to our insurance people, and they said they'd never seen this before," she said, adding that roughly 90 percent of her dryland cotton was dead.
Many of these ephemeral lakes were dry in September 2026, unlike the previous year.

B1-B2.headline: Texas Cotton Farmers Facing Drought

pages.text: Cotton farmers in the Texas High Plains are facing a catastrophic drought in 2026. While the region has experienced dry seasons before, such as in 2022 and 2011, this year feels different.
pages.caption: A satellite image of the same Lubbock region on September 9, 2026, appears parched, with much less green vegetation and mostly dry lakes.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Drought Monitor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln

pages.text: Many farmers report that their crops have completely died, with some losing up to 90 percent of their dryland cotton. Satellite imagery from Landsat 8 shows a stark contrast between the green, healthy fields of 2025 and the parched, brown landscape of 2026.
pages.caption: A satellite image of farmland around Lubbock, Texas, on September 22, 2025, features a patchwork of green and brown agricultural fields and several playa lakes with varying amounts of water.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Drought Monitor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln

pages.text: Because groundwater is becoming scarce, farmers are irrigating smaller portions of their fields, which appear as green shapes in satellite photos. The region relies on the High Plains aquifer, but water levels have dropped significantly since 1950. Many shallow water features, known as playa lakes, are also dry.

These lakes are vital because they help recharge the aquifer. Unfortunately, about 80 percent of these lakes are damaged by farming activities. As the water table continues to decline, many irrigation wells have stopped working, leaving farmers without a backup water source.

evidence: Miserably dry seasons forced farmers in America's largest cotton-producing region to abandon massive portions of their dryland crop, including 72 percent in 2022 and 66 percent in 2011.
Note also the many shallow water features known as playa lakes —sometimes called mud holes, buffalo wallows, and lagoons—scattered throughout the image.
Farmers in this region operate along the eastern margin of the aquifer, which has declined sharply in recent decades.

C1-C2.headline: Texas Cotton Country Faces Water Stress

pages.text: The 2026 drought in the Texas High Plains has transcended historical precedents, manifesting in unprecedented crop failure for local cotton producers. Farmers who previously navigated severe dry spells in 2011 and 2022 now confront a landscape where dryland cotton has perished entirely. Satellite analysis via the Landsat 8 OLI sensor corroborates this degradation, revealing a transition from the verdant, productive fields observed in 2025 to the desiccated, vacant plots that characterized the region by September 2026.
pages.caption: A satellite image of the same Lubbock region on September 9, 2026, appears parched, with much less green vegetation and mostly dry lakes.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Drought Monitor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln

pages.text: The crisis is exacerbated by the long-term depletion of the High Plains aquifer. Geological Survey data indicates that the water table has receded by 25 to 100 feet in Lubbock County since 1950, with more extreme declines recorded in northern counties. This systemic water scarcity has rendered many irrigation wells non-functional, forcing farmers to abandon traditional cultivation methods.
pages.caption: A satellite image of farmland around Lubbock, Texas, on September 22, 2025, features a patchwork of green and brown agricultural fields and several playa lakes with varying amounts of water.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Drought Monitor at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln

pages.text: Furthermore, the degradation of playa lakes—ephemeral, clay-lined basins—has compromised the natural recharge pathways essential for aquifer sustainability. With approximately 80 percent of these features modified by sediment or tilling, their capacity to mitigate water stress is severely diminished. In response, agricultural conservationists are collaborating with research consortia like NASA Acres to implement adaptive strategies.

These initiatives prioritize water-efficient techniques and the restoration of playa lakes to preserve the remaining groundwater. Despite recent precipitation, meteorologists emphasize that the current moisture levels remain insufficient to alleviate the drought's structural impact. As the aquifer continues to decline, the agricultural community faces an urgent imperative to innovate, as the traditional reliance on groundwater is no longer a viable long-term strategy for the region's survival.

evidence: But in some ways, farmers felt the drought in 2026 entered new territory.

Geological Survey data , the water table across much of Lubbock County has dropped by between 25 and 100 feet since 1950, around when people began drawing large volumes of water from the aquifer to irrigate.
The aquifer's long-term decline, combined with the 2026 drought, left many wells "pumping air" this summer for some of the farmers Timmons-Sims knows.

A1-A2.headline: Hurricane Simon Near Mexican Coast

pages.text: Hurricane Simon is a big storm. It was a category 4 storm on October 11, 2026. It moved near the coast of Mexico. The wind was very fast. It reached 250 kilometers per hour. The storm was 50 kilometers from the land.
pages.caption: The well-defined eye of Hurricane Simon lies just off Mexico’s Pacific coast. Some outer cloud bands of the spiraling storm extend over land.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)

pages.text: It was between two cities. These cities are Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta. A satellite took a picture of the storm. The mountains helped make the storm smaller. But the storm brought a lot of rain. There was flooding in Manzanillo.

People were worried about mudslides in the mountains. Satellites saw waves in the air. These waves are high up in the sky. They happen when the storm is very strong. The moon was not very bright that night.
pages.caption: Gravity waves in the upper atmosphere appear as a semicircle of ripples in a nighttime, grayscale satellite image. Hurricane clouds and city lights in Mexico are also visible.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)

pages.text: This helped the camera see the waves. Experts do not know where the storm will go. They have low confidence in their plans. The storm might go to the Gulf of California. The water near the coast is dangerous now.

evidence: Hurricane Simon, the latest in a long progression of tropical cyclones in the Eastern Pacific this season, passed close to the Mexican coast as a category 4 storm on October 11, 2026.
Sustained winds reached 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour as it crept north-northwest.

Still, the major hurricane delivered heavy rain and flooding to coastal areas, including the port city of Manzanillo, and raised the risk of mudslides in mountainous areas, according to news reports .

B1-B2.headline: Hurricane Simon Passes Mexican Coast

pages.text: Hurricane Simon, a powerful tropical cyclone, moved near the Mexican coast as a category 4 storm on October 11, 2026. As it traveled north-northwest, sustained winds reached 250 kilometers per hour. By the time the Suomi NPP satellite captured an image at 2:30 p.m., the eye of the storm was 50 kilometers offshore between Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.
pages.caption: The well-defined eye of Hurricane Simon lies just off Mexico’s Pacific coast. Some outer cloud bands of the spiraling storm extend over land.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)

pages.text: The National Hurricane Center reported that sustained winds had decreased to 210 kilometers per hour as the inner core brushed the coast. The Sierra Madre mountains helped temper the storm's intensity and reduced its wind field. Despite this, the hurricane caused significant flooding in Manzanillo and increased the risk of mudslides in mountainous regions.

Advanced satellite technology also observed atmospheric gravity waves radiating from the storm. These ripples occur when latent heat near the eyewall creates strong convection, pushing air into the stratosphere. While these waves are often difficult to detect, minimal moonlight allowed the VIIRS sensor to capture them clearly as ripples in airglow.
pages.caption: Gravity waves in the upper atmosphere appear as a semicircle of ripples in a nighttime, grayscale satellite image. Hurricane clouds and city lights in Mexico are also visible.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)

pages.text: As of October 13, meteorologists maintained very low confidence regarding the storm's future path. The system may move north into the Gulf of California. Meanwhile, authorities have warned that large swells will create dangerous conditions along the southwestern and west-central coasts of Mexico.

evidence: By that time, sustained winds were about 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), and the storm’s inner core was brushing up against the coast.
The topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper the storm’s intensity somewhat and shrink the size of its wind field, the NHC noted.
On the morning of October 13, forecasts of Simon’s intensity and path remained “very low confidence,” as the storm’s evolution continued to defy meteorologists’ expectations .

C1-C2.headline: Hurricane Simon Delivers Coastal Flooding

pages.text: On October 11, 2026, Hurricane Simon, a formidable category 4 tropical cyclone, tracked in close proximity to the Mexican coastline. The system, characterized by sustained winds of 250 kilometers per hour, exhibited a north-northwest trajectory. Data acquired by the Suomi NPP satellite at 2:30 p.m. local time placed the eye of the storm approximately 50 kilometers offshore, situated between the coastal hubs of Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.
pages.caption: The well-defined eye of Hurricane Simon lies just off Mexico’s Pacific coast. Some outer cloud bands of the spiraling storm extend over land.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)

pages.text: The National Hurricane Center observed that the storm’s interaction with the rugged topography of the Sierra Madre mountains served to mitigate its intensity, effectively constricting the wind field. Nevertheless, the meteorological event precipitated severe rainfall and inundation in Manzanillo, while simultaneously elevating the probability of catastrophic mudslides throughout the mountainous interior.

Beyond surface-level impacts, satellite imagery from the NOAA-21 platform revealed atmospheric gravity waves emanating from the hurricane. These phenomena are generated when latent heat release near the eyewall triggers vigorous convection, propelling updrafts into the stratosphere and mesosphere. Although these ripples are frequently obscured by upper-atmospheric winds or reflected lunar illumination, the specific conditions on October 11—characterized by minimal moonlight—facilitated the observation of these waves within the airglow.
pages.caption: Gravity waves in the upper atmosphere appear as a semicircle of ripples in a nighttime, grayscale satellite image. Hurricane clouds and city lights in Mexico are also visible.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE, GIBS/Worldview, the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership, and the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)

pages.text: As of October 13, the storm’s evolution continued to defy established meteorological models, resulting in forecasts of very low confidence. The system’s potential progression into the Gulf of California remains a subject of uncertainty. Consequently, coastal regions along the southwestern and west-central Mexican littoral are bracing for large swells and hazardous nearshore conditions, as the system’s ultimate landfall remains indeterminate.

evidence: In the early morning hours of October 11, satellites captured the storm’s effects extending into the upper atmosphere .

These ripples form when latent heat released near the tropical cyclone’s eyewall drives strong convection, building tall cumulonimbus clouds with updrafts that can send waves into the stratosphere and mesosphere.
The system may steer north and enter the Gulf of California before making landfall.

A1-A2.headline: Floodwaters in Thailand After Heavy Rains

pages.text: Thailand has a rainy season in September. People there know about rain. But this year, the rain was very heavy. It did not stop for many days. Many places in the country are now under water.
pages.caption: Floodwaters along the Bang Pakong River, 2 October 2026 (false-color NASA Landsat image).

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

pages.text: Prachin Buri is one place with big floods. NASA satellites took pictures of the land. The pictures show water on farms and near the Bang Pakong River. The water covers the land on October 2, 2026.
pages.caption: Bang Pakong River area in October 2025, before the 2026 flood (false-color NASA Landsat image).

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

pages.text: A weather system stayed over the area for a long time. It brought a lot of water from the Gulf of Thailand. Bangkok had 300 millimeters of rain in 48 hours.

This is almost as much as the rain for the whole month. Floods are in 50 provinces now. More than 4 million people have problems. Sadly, many people died. The water also hurt 270,000 hectares of farms. Farmers lost rice and fruit.

evidence: September falls in the heart of the monsoon season in Thailand, where cities and towns are accustomed to the afternoon rains and thunderstorms that frequently roll through.
Prachin Buri province was among the areas where flooding was widespread.

Since mid-September, flooding has occurred in 50 provinces across the country, affecting over 4 million people and causing dozens of deaths, according to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies .

B1-B2.headline: Thailand Floodwaters Inundate Farmland

pages.text: Thailand is currently experiencing severe flooding following a period of persistent heavy rainfall. While the country is accustomed to monsoon rains during September, the intensity of the downpours between late September and early October 2026 has been exceptional, leading to sustained flooding across many low-lying regions.
pages.caption: Floodwaters along the Bang Pakong River, 2 October 2026 (false-color NASA Landsat image).

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

pages.text: Satellite imagery from NASA-USGS Landsat satellites highlights the scale of the disaster. In Prachin Buri province, images taken on October 2, 2026, reveal that land along the Bang Pakong River, including agricultural areas and aquaculture facilities, remains inundated. These false-color images allow experts to clearly distinguish between water and land surfaces.
pages.caption: Bang Pakong River area in October 2025, before the 2026 flood (false-color NASA Landsat image).

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

pages.text: Meteorologists suggest that a stalled low-pressure system is responsible for the deluge. This system drew moisture from the warm Gulf of Thailand, resulting in extreme rainfall. For instance, Bangkok recorded nearly 300 millimeters of rain within a 48-hour period, which is nearly equivalent to the typical monthly total of 344 millimeters.

The humanitarian impact is significant. According to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, flooding has affected 50 provinces and over 4 million people, resulting in dozens of deaths. Furthermore, government agencies report that approximately 270,000 hectares of farmland, including vital rice fields and fruit orchards, have suffered extensive damage.

evidence: But throughout late September and early October 2026, persistent heavy rains punctuated by intense downpours left low-lying areas across the country in Southeast Asia under sustained flooding.
The right image above shows land along the Bang Pakong River and nearby agricultural areas and aquaculture facilities inundated on October 2, 2026.
Government agencies estimate about 270,000 hectares (670,000 acres) of farmland, including rice fields and fruit orchards, have been damaged.

C1-C2.headline: Floodwaters Overwhelm Thailand Farmland

pages.text: Thailand is currently grappling with the aftermath of a protracted meteorological event that has left vast swathes of the nation submerged. Although the country typically experiences a monsoon season in September, the period spanning late September to early October 2026 was characterized by relentless, high-intensity precipitation that overwhelmed local infrastructure and left low-lying regions in a state of sustained inundation.
pages.caption: Floodwaters along the Bang Pakong River, 2 October 2026 (false-color NASA Landsat image).

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

pages.text: Remote sensing data acquired by NASA-USGS Landsat satellites provides a stark visual record of the devastation. Comparative analysis of imagery from Prachin Buri province—contrasting October 2, 2026, with the same period in 2025—illustrates the extent to which the Bang Pakong River basin and adjacent aquaculture facilities have been compromised. The use of false-color rendering facilitates the precise identification of water encroachment upon developed and agricultural land.
pages.caption: Bang Pakong River area in October 2025, before the 2026 flood (false-color NASA Landsat image).

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey

pages.text: The meteorological catalyst for this crisis appears to be a stationary low-pressure system. Fueled by the thermal energy and moisture of the Gulf of Thailand, this system deposited an extraordinary volume of rain. Bangkok, for example, received nearly 300 millimeters of precipitation in a mere 48-hour window, a figure that approaches the 344-millimeter average for the entire month of September. The socio-economic repercussions are profound.

Data from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies indicates that 50 provinces have been impacted, with over 4 million individuals affected and a tragic toll of dozens of fatalities. The agricultural sector has been particularly hard hit; government estimates suggest that 270,000 hectares of productive land, encompassing essential rice paddies and fruit orchards, have sustained significant damage, threatening regional food security.

evidence: Acquired with NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, the images are false-color to better distinguish water from vegetation, developed land, and other surfaces.
Some of the flooding likely stemmed from a low-pressure system that stalled over the area for several days in late September.
Stoked by moisture and energy from the warm Gulf of Thailand nearby, the system delivered especially intense rains to the region.

A1-A2.headline: Fires Burn in Amazon Rainforest

pages.text: The Amazon rainforest is very dry this year. A weather event called El Niño causes this dry weather. Scientists say a long fire season is starting now. Fires started in September 2026. They are near the cities of Manaus and Santarém.
pages.caption: Thick gray smoke partially obscures the Amazon River and surrounding rainforest near the cities of Manaus and Santarém. Puffy white clouds rise above the smoke on the left side of the image.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

pages.text: Satellites see smoke from space. The smoke is bad for the air in Manaus. More than 2 million people live there. Schools closed because the air is not safe. Most fires start because of people.

People use fire to clear land for farms. The dry weather makes the fires grow fast. The fires burn the forest floor. This is bad for the trees and animals. Scientists see a pattern. First, there are fires in Indonesia.

Then, there are fires in the Amazon. This happened in 2015, 2023, and now in 2026. Experts think the fires will move to other areas soon. They will burn until the rain comes in December 2026 or January 2027.

evidence: This year, a drought accompanying El Niño has left the Amazon rainforest primed to burn, and scientists say the region has entered the early stages of what they think will be a long and severe fire season.
The pall disrupted daily life in a city of more than 2 million people.
Schools closed, and citywide events and children's sports leagues were canceled as officials warned of hazardous air quality, according to news reports .

B1-B2.headline: Amazon Rainforest Fires and Drought

pages.text: The Amazon rainforest is currently experiencing a severe fire season driven by a drought linked to El Niño. Unlike short-lived weather events, El Niño impacts the region over many months, leaving the forest highly vulnerable to fire. Since September 2026, satellite data has shown a significant increase in fire activity and smoke emissions, particularly near the cities of Manaus and Santarém.
pages.caption: Thick gray smoke partially obscures the Amazon River and surrounding rainforest near the cities of Manaus and Santarém. Puffy white clouds rise above the smoke on the left side of the image.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

pages.text: On October 12, 2026, heavy smoke covered Manaus, where over 2 million people reside. Air quality became hazardous, with fine particulate matter (PM 2.5) levels exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. Consequently, local authorities closed schools and canceled public events to protect citizens from the poor air quality. Scientists describe this as a "cascade" of fire.

The pattern typically begins with drought and peat fires in Indonesia, followed by increased fire activity in the Amazon. This sequence was observed during the 2015–2016 and 2023 El Niño events. Experts warn that many of these forests are burning again, which causes significant ecological damage because local species are not adapted to fire.

Most of these fires are human-caused, often starting as land-clearing efforts that escape control. Because the forest is so dry, these fires spread easily through the understory. Scientists expect the fires near Manaus and Santarém to persist until the rainy season begins in December 2026 or January 2027. Meanwhile, researchers are working to identify additional fires that satellites might miss due to dense smoke and cloud cover.

evidence: The region with elevated fire activity stretches from forests surrounding the commercial and transportation centers of Manaus and Santarém to the mouth of the Amazon River.

That day, city officials reported extremely poor air quality, with fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) values above 135 micrograms per cubic meter, the second-worst rating on a regional air quality index .
Forest fires in these rainforests are known to cause especially serious ecological damage because most species are not adapted to fire.

C1-C2.headline: Amazon Rainforest Enters Early Fire Season

pages.text: The Amazon rainforest is currently enduring a protracted and severe fire season, a phenomenon exacerbated by the persistent drought conditions associated with the 2026 El Niño. While transient weather events like thunderstorms deliver immediate, localized impacts, El Niño exerts a sustained influence that has rendered the Amazonian ecosystem exceptionally susceptible to ignition.
pages.caption: Thick gray smoke partially obscures the Amazon River and surrounding rainforest near the cities of Manaus and Santarém. Puffy white clouds rise above the smoke on the left side of the image.

imageProvenance.credit: NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview

pages.text: Satellite monitoring platforms, including NASA’s FIRMS and GFED, have documented a sharp escalation in fire activity and smoke emissions since September 2026, with the most intense activity concentrated between the commercial hubs of Manaus and Santarém. The environmental degradation reached a critical threshold on October 12, 2026, when dense smoke blanketed Manaus. Air quality indices recorded fine particulate matter (PM 2.5) concentrations exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter, prompting the suspension of educational and recreational activities for the city’s 2 million inhabitants.

This atmospheric crisis is part of a broader tropical fire cascade; scientists have identified a recurring pattern where drought-induced peat fires in Indonesia precede elevated fire activity in the Amazon, a sequence previously documented during the 2015–2016 and 2023 El Niño cycles. Ecologically, these fires are particularly catastrophic as the indigenous flora and fauna lack evolutionary adaptations to fire.

Furthermore, the recurrence of fires in previously charred areas has degraded the forest structure, rendering the remaining vegetation increasingly flammable. Douglas Morton of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center notes that while these fires often originate from agricultural management practices, they have escaped containment, spreading rapidly through the parched understory. Current satellite analysis suggests that official counts may underestimate the true extent of the conflagration, as dense smoke and canopy cover frequently obscure infrared signals from sensors.

Looking ahead, researchers anticipate the fire front will migrate northward toward Roraima, northern Pará, and Amapá, as well as neighboring nations, before peaking in the southern Amazon by late 2027. While the current fires near Manaus are expected to persist until the onset of the rainy season in December 2026 or January 2027, experts emphasize that proactive mitigation remains critical for regions yet to be impacted.

evidence: Unlike a tornado or thunderstorm that can deliver destruction in minutes, El Niño exerts its influence over many months.
"Now, in the Amazon, we're seeing the second domino in the cascade fall," Morton said, referring to the uptick in fires that has begun in Pará and Amazonas.

It's likely that some of the forest fires will burn even more intensely this time because the earlier fires partially charred trees, degrading the forest and making what remained more susceptible to burning, he added.

pages.text: The Amazon rainforest is currently experiencing a severe fire season driven by a drought linked to El Niño. Unlike short-lived weather events, El Niño impacts the region over many months, leaving the forest highly vulnerable to fire. Since September 2026, satellite data has shown a significant increase in fire activity and smoke emissions, particularly near the cities of Manaus and Santarém.

pages.text: On October 12, 2026, heavy smoke covered Manaus, where over 2 million people reside. Air quality became hazardous, with fine particulate matter (PM 2.5) levels exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. Consequently, local authorities closed schools and canceled public events to protect citizens from the poor air quality. Scientists describe this as a "cascade" of fire.

The pattern typically begins with drought and peat fires in Indonesia, followed by increased fire activity in the Amazon. This sequence was observed during the 2015–2016 and 2023 El Niño events. Experts warn that many of these forests are burning again, which causes significant ecological damage because local species are not adapted to fire.

Most of these fires are human-caused, often starting as land-clearing efforts that escape control. Because the forest is so dry, these fires spread easily through the understory. Scientists expect the fires near Manaus and Santarém to persist until the rainy season begins in December 2026 or January 2027. Meanwhile, researchers are working to identify additional fires that satellites might miss due to dense smoke and cloud cover.
